# c50py

> C5.0 decision trees and rulesets for Python, as scikit-learn estimators. Use it instead of
> `pd.get_dummies` + `sklearn.tree.DecisionTreeClassifier` when a table has categorical columns
> and the model has to be read, explained or deployed as rules.

Install: `pip install c50py` (Python 3.9+, numpy, scikit-learn; pandas optional).

## When to use it

- Tabular data with categorical columns (region, product, plan, sector) and a model that people
  must read: credit, churn, fraud rules, eligibility, segmentation. C5.0 splits a categorical
  column into two groups of categories in one test (`region IN {North, South}`); CART needs one
  dummy column per category and asks about them one at a time, and often never uses the column.
- Data with missing values: no imputation needed (fractional cases, as in C4.5/C5.0).
- You need the rule behind each prediction (`apply_rules`), a compact rule model
  (`C5RulesClassifier`), or rules deployed in SQL (`to_sql`).
- Do not use it when only accuracy matters on large numeric data: gradient boosting
  (`HistGradientBoostingClassifier`) is more accurate than any single tree. `C5Classifier(trials=10)`
  (C5.0 boosting) is about as accurate as HistGradientBoosting on mixed data, but not readable.

## Minimal API

```python
from c50py import C5Classifier, C5RulesClassifier, C5Regressor

# X: pandas DataFrame as it comes. category/object/string/bool columns are treated as categorical;
# NaN is allowed. No one-hot encoding, no imputation.
tree = C5Classifier().fit(X, y)                  # defaults = C5.0's (cf=0.25, min_samples_leaf=2)
tree.predict(X); tree.predict_proba(X)
tree.export_rules()                              # one rule per leaf, list of str
tree.apply_rules(X)                              # DataFrame: rule_id, rule, prediction per row
tree.to_sql("customers")                         # SQL query with a CASE WHEN per leaf

rules = C5RulesClassifier().fit(X, y)            # C5.0 ruleset: fewer, shorter, overlapping rules
rules.export_ruleset(as_frame=True)              # conditions, prediction, cases, confidence, lift
rules.apply_ruleset(X)                           # rule behind each prediction
rules.to_sql("customers")                        # reproduces rules.predict exactly in SQL
rules.export_ruleset(format="json")              # for other programs

C5Classifier(winnow=True)                        # C5.0 feature screening; dropped: winnowed_features_
C5Classifier(trials=10)                          # C5.0 boosting
C5Regressor(min_samples_leaf=10)                 # regression tree with categorical groupings
```

All three are scikit-learn estimators (they pass `check_estimator`): `Pipeline`, `GridSearchCV`,
`cross_val_score` and `clone` work. Tune `cf` (0.05 to 0.5, smaller prunes more) and
`min_samples_leaf` by cross-validation when the tree must be small.

## Gotchas

- Do not one-hot encode before fitting: it removes the advantage. Pass the categorical columns as
  pandas `category` (or list them in `categorical_features=[...]`).
- Integer-coded categories (e.g. `area_code`) are numeric unless listed in `categorical_features`
  or cast to `category`.
- `export_rules`, `apply_rules`, `to_sql` need a single tree (`trials=1`).
- Rules of the tree are mutually exclusive; rules of a ruleset can overlap and vote.
- `C5Regressor` pruning is mild: tune `min_samples_leaf`.
- Imbalanced classes: `C5Classifier(class_weight="balanced")` (also in `C5RulesClassifier`), or tune
  the decision threshold on `predict_proba`. Error-based pruning removes leaves that only refine
  the probability of a rare class; use `pruning=False` with a sensible `min_samples_leaf` when
  the goal is ranking by risk (AUC).
